e.etymology: The usual English spelling of Maud, from Old French Mahaut, the medieval spoken form of Matilda. Matilda joins Germanic words for might and battle.
namesakes: Maude Findlay (Bea Arthur's title character in the 1970s sitcom Maude)

e.etymology: The French and German form of Helen, from Greek Helene, the name of Helen of Troy. The Greek name is usually linked to a word for a torch or bright light.

assoc.t: hurricane that struck Florida and North Carolina in 2024

e.etymology: In Sweden a 19th-century feminine form of Alf, elf, now a top girls' name there. In older American use it was mostly a man's name, a spelling of Biblical Alvah, as in Thomas Alva Edison.
namesakes: Thomas Alva Edison (inventor; Alva was his middle name)

e.etymology: A respelling of Jeremiah, from Hebrew Yirmeyahu, the Lord exalts, the name of the Old Testament prophet.
From Old High German gisal, pledge, the word for a noble child raised at another court to seal an alliance. Giselle is the French form.
A respelling of Charlotte, the French feminine form of Charles, from Germanic karl, free man.
An American nickname for Charles or Christopher, often given to a son who shares his father's name, a chip off the old block.
namesakes: Chip Gaines (co-host of HGTV's Fixer Upper)
Chip (the teacup in Disney's Beauty and the Beast)

assoc.t: the everyday word: potato chip, computer chip

e.etymology: A form of Adamari, a name made familiar to Spanish-speaking Americans by Puerto Rican actress and TV host Adamari Lopez. It resembles Ada joined to Damaris; no meaning is established.
A modern American name in the pattern of Makayla, Zakiya and Maliyah. It has no established meaning.
The English words baby girl written as one. In birth records it appears largely as a placeholder for a newborn who had not yet been named.

assoc.t: baby girl, an everyday term of endearment

e.note: Mostly a pet name and a hospital-form placeholder, not a given name; it will be read as a term of endearment.

e.etymology: The French feminine form of Emmanuel, from Hebrew Immanuel, God is with us, the name spoken in Isaiah's prophecy.

assoc.t: Emmanuelle, the 1974 French erotic film and its sequels

e.note: Emmanuelle is also the title of a long-running series of French erotic films that began in 1974.

e.etymology: An Irish surname from O hAgain, descendant of Ogan, a pet form of og, young. Some families trace it instead to O hAodhagain, from aodh, fire.
A modern American name in the family of Keelan, Kylan and Kaylen. The spelling can be read more than one way and has no single established source.
A modern American name, a clipped form of Kamryn (Cameron) with the -i ending of Kali and Demi.
e.note: Sounds exactly like Camry, the Toyota sedan.

e.etymology: The Hebrew form of Rebecca, wife of Isaac and mother of Jacob and Esau. It comes from a Semitic root meaning to tie firmly, often read as captivating.
A respelling of Preston, an English place name and surname from Old English preost, priest, and tun, settlement.
The West African form of Adam, given to both boys and girls in Mali, Senegal and Guinea. Adam is Hebrew for man and is tied to adamah, the Hebrew word for earth or ground.
A phonetic spelling of Alize, from French alizé, the trade wind. Pakistani families also use it alongside Alizeh.
e.note: Sounds the same as Alizé, a French cognac liqueur brand sold widely in the US.

e.etymology: A Yiddish name, also spelled Baila or Beyle, usually traced to a Romance word for beautiful, as in Bella. Some link it instead to a Slavic word for white.
The Italian form of Julian, from Latin Iulianus, belonging to Julius, the Roman family of Julius Caesar.
A modern American elaboration in the family of Aviana and Avion, with the -onna ending of Brionna. It has no established meaning.
Used mainly in Spanish-speaking families, alongside Mailen and Maylin. It is probably a form of Mailén, a name from Chile and Argentina said to come from a Mapuche word for girl or maiden.
An English surname, a form of the Yorkshire place name Helmsley. As a girls' name it follows Ainsley and Paisley, with the Em- of Emma and Emily.
A respelling of Josiah, from Hebrew Yoshiyahu, the Lord supports, the name of a reforming king of Judah in the Old Testament.
An Igbo name from amara, grace, and Chi, God: the grace of God.
In the US mostly a girls' name among Zomi (Chin) families from Myanmar, where Cing is a common first element of women's names.
In the US mostly a respelling of Seven, the number used as a name. Sevin is separately a Turkish name from the verb for to love or rejoice.
e.note: Sevin is also a long-sold brand of garden insecticide.

e.etymology: The Armenian and Eastern European form of Arsenius, from Greek arsen, male or manly. Saint Arsenius the Great was a desert monk of the 5th century.
e.note: Said AR-sen, it sounds very close to the English word arson.

e.etymology: A French place name and surname from beau, beautiful, and regard, view or outlook. It became a Southern given name in honor of Confederate general P. G. T. Beauregard.
e.note: Strongly Southern in feel and tied to a Confederate general.

e.etymology: The English word for the power to attract, from Old French aleurer, to lure, originally a falconry term for calling a hawk back with bait.
From Arabic lujayn, a literary word for silver.
A double-n spelling of Luna, the Latin, Spanish and Italian word for the moon and the name of the Roman moon goddess.
